# The retired authority sentences.
#
# Each entry below is one sentence the documentation used to carry, in the
# bytes it carried, and dinah-495 retired every one of them. They asserted
# that the operator alone can do a thing, or that an act belongs to him, and
# each was replaced by a description of the refusal Dinah performs. The
# difference is that the refusal is true as written: the actor ladder puts the
# `--actor` flag above the environment and the config, so any caller presents
# the operator's name for the cost of one flag, and a caller who can write the
# files under `.dinah` settles an item with an editor and no verb at all.
#
# TestNoRetiredAuthoritySentenceStandsInTheDocumentation reads this file. It
# flattens each document to single spaces before searching, so a re-wrap, a
# reflow, or a copy pasted back at a different column width still fails. What
# it keys on is the retired bytes, which is what makes it unevadable for the
# sentences it holds.
#
# The last three entries are the owner flag's help text, which is this card's
# narrower instance. The first two are what dinah-206 wrote and dinah-484 left
# standing. The third is what this card wrote in their place on its first pass,
# and it is here because it carried the same defect in new words: strip it and
# what is left is "settling such an item is the operator's", which is the shape
# the nineteen above were retired for. It was copied out of the design
# document's own sentence, which says that much and then continues past a colon
# with the refusal that makes it true, and only the first half travelled.
#
# What it does not cover, and this is the limit worth meeting here rather than
# discovering later. The ledger holds these twenty-five sentences and nothing
# else. Add `Only the operator can rename a column.` to
# internal/guide/guides/verbs.md and the suite stays green, because no check
# in the tree recognises the claim, only these strings. Recognising the claim
# would mean recognising a claim rather than a string, and the string-shaped
# approximations are a list of forbidden phrasings, which fits only the
# phrasings somebody thought of, or a ledger over all 141 operator-mentioning
# sentences of the twelve documents. dinah-495 D-6 records that call. The
# ledger also holds English bytes alone, so a retired sentence returning as a
# translation of itself is not found.
#
# A line opening with `#` is a comment and a blank line is ignored. Every
# other line is one entry, flattened to single spaces exactly as the search
# flattens the documents.

The operator holds acts nobody else may take.
A block frees the card and records why, and only the operator lifts one.
Dinah assigns an operator to every workbench, the person who owns it and answers for it, and only that operator may lift a block, so a workbench with nobody in that seat has actions nobody can perform.
The `operator_owned` flag on a column is the answer to whether that column is yours to move cards out of, and it repeats the rule in `initialize`.
A card you name must exist, a card another owner holds is not yours to claim, and a card in an operator-owned column is not yours to move.
Only the operator lifts a block, with `dinah unblock <card>`.
Writing a hold is the operator's, the way every other write to a column is; reading it is open to anybody.
A column may declare a limit on how much work it holds, and a move into a full column is refused; the operator may carry one through with `--override`, which is recorded on the move.
`unblock` lifts a block, and only the operator may do it.
Only the operator can lift a block or force a move past a limit.
You want that second answer, because Dinah lets the operator do things it will not let anybody else do.
It reads `agent` for a column anybody can work and `operator` for one where the departure is the operator's alone, and you choose the second by writing `operator_owned: true` into the column's own file.
Only the operator can carry a card through a full column, and Dinah records the override:
Only the operator can lift a block.
A workstream that already exists can still be renamed, and that write belongs to the operator rather than to whoever created it.
The invariants: `active` and the presence of claim fields imply each other; `blocked` carries a reason and is cleared only by the operator; `ready` means pullable.
Clearing a block is the operator's act and is journaled.
A column marked operator-owned is one an agent never moves a card out of; only the operator does.
A column may declare both, and then the workbench waits there and only the operator moves the card onward.
who the item is meant for, recorded on the item and never enforced
It says the value is recorded rather than checked, so a reader does not take it for an authorisation.
who the item is meant for; an item whose owner reads operator is the workbench operator's to settle

# The three entries below were retired on dinah-582, and for a different
# reason than every entry above them. Those were retired because they
# overstated what the tool guarantees: the refusal they described was real and
# the sentence claimed more than a name comparison can deliver. These three
# were true when they were written and the operator's ruling of 2026-09-23
# made them false. A workstream's fields, built-in and declared alike, are any
# owner's to write, so a sentence saying such a write is refused to everybody
# but the operator now describes a refusal the tool does not perform. A reader
# who applies dinah-495's rationale to these three has the wrong reason for
# the right entry.
#
# The quick-start entry is the second sentence that file has had retired on
# this subject. The first, "A workstream that already exists can still be
# renamed, and that write belongs to the operator rather than to whoever
# created it.", stands above and is not superseded: it was retired for
# dinah-495's reason and its replacement is retired here for this one.
Dinah refuses a write of the hold to any actor but the operator, and it refuses every other write to a column, to the workbench's own fields and to a workstream's on the same rule; reading any of them is open to anybody.
A workstream that already exists can still be renamed, and Dinah refuses that write to every actor but the operator, whoever created the workstream.
They are changing a field of the workbench itself or of a workstream, anything done to an attachment of the workbench, archiving, restoring, or deleting a column, and running `reshape`.
